chapters.title: Prehistory
chapters.summary: In the case of Senegal, the periodization of prehistory remains controversial. It is often described as beginning with the age of metallurgy, thus placing it between the first metalworking and the appearance of writing.

Lower Paleolithic presence is attested by Acheulean tools such as hand axes reported by Théodore Monod at Fann in Cap-Vert in 1938 and cleavers in the south-east [S2]. The Neolithic deposit Manueline Dakar at Cape Manuel was discovered in 1940 and proto-historic ruins in the middle Senegal River valley were confirmed in the late 1970s [S2]. Guy Thilmans and his team in 1980 felt any pre-colonial archeology could be attached to that designation and Hamady Bocoum speaks of Historical Archaeology from the 4th century for former Tekrur [S2]. The Stone Circles of Senegambia in nearly 33,000 km2 around the Gambia were listed by UNESCO in 2006 [S2].

chapters.title: Early historical inhabitants
chapters.summary: In the absence of written sources and monumental ruins in this region, the history of the early centuries of the modern era must be based primarily on archaeological excavations, the writing of early Arab geographers and travelers, and data derived from oral tradition. Combining these data suggests that Senegal was first populated from the north and east in several waves of migration, the last being that of the Wolof, the Fulani and the Serer who dominate the area today.
chapters.narrative: The provided excerpt reflects a single synthesized perspective on this period. In the absence of written sources and monumental ruins in this region, the history of the early centuries of the modern era must be based primarily on archaeological excavations, the writing of early Arab geographers and travelers, and data derived from oral tradition [S3]. Combining these data suggests that Senegal was first populated from the north and east in several waves of migration [S3]. The last being that of the Wolof, the Fulani and the Serer who dominate the area today [S3]. Oral tradition is cited alongside archaeology and Arab geographers as a primary basis for this history [S3].

chapters.title: Kingdoms and empires
chapters.summary: The medieval history of the Sahel is characterized by the consolidation of settlements into large state entities – the Ghana Empire, the Mali Empire and the Songhai Empire. The cores of these great empires were located on the territory of the current Republic of Mali, so current-day Senegal occupied a peripheral position.

events.label: 9th c.
events.text: Its existence in the 9th century is attested by Arabic manuscripts.

John Donnelly Fage suggests that Takrur was formed through the interaction of Berbers from the Sahara and "Negro agricultural peoples" who were "essentially Serer" although its kings after 1000 CE might have been Soninke (northern Mande).
The Tekrur were among the first converts to Islam, certainly before 1040.

events.label: 13th c.
events.text: In Casamance, the Baïnounks, the Manjaques and Diola inhabited the coastal area while the mainland – unified 13th century under the name of Kaabu – was occupied by the Mandingo.

events.label: 14th c.
events.text: Two other major political entities were formed and grew during the 13th and 14th century: the Mali Empire and the Jolof Empire which become the vassal of the first in its heyday.

events.label: 15th c.
events.text: In the 15th century, the king of one of the tribes, Kassas gave his name to the region: Kassa Mansa (King of Kassas).

Djolof expanded its dominance of small chiefdoms south of the Senegal River (Waalo, Cayor, Baol, Sine – Saloum), bringing together all the Senegambia to which he gave religious and social unity: the "Grand Djolof"   which collapsed in 1550.

chapters.narrative: The Sahel history is characterized by consolidation into Ghana, Mali and Songhai empires whose cores were on territory of current Mali, so Senegal occupied peripheral position [S4]. Its existence in 9th century is attested by Arabic manuscripts [S4]. Takrur was formed through interaction of Berbers and agricultural peoples essentially Serer although kings after 1000 CE might have been Soninke [S4]. Tekrur were among first converts to Islam before 1040 [S4]. In Casamance Baïnounks, Manjaques and Diola inhabited coastal area while mainland unified in 13th century as Kaabu was occupied by Mandingo [S4]. Mali and Jolof empires grew during 13th and 14th century and Jolof became vassal of Mali [S4]. Grand Djolof collapsed in 1550 [S4]. The excerpts reflect a state-centered and external-source perspective [S4].

chapters.title: The era of trading posts and trafficking
chapters.summary: According to several ancient sources, including occasions by the Dictionnaire de pédagogie et d'instruction primaire by Ferdinand Buisson in 1887, the first French settlement in Senegal dates back to the Dieppe Mariners in the 14th century. Flattering for Norman sailors, this argument gives credence also to the idea of a precedence of the French presence in the region, but it is not confirmed by subsequent work.

events.text: After the Act of Abjuration in 1581, the United Provinces flouted the authority of the King of Spain.
In 1626 Richelieu founded the Norman Company, an association of Dieppe and Rouen merchants responsible for the operation in Senegal and the Gambia.
They also traversed the lower Casamance and founded Ziguinchor in 1645.

events.label: 17th c.
events.text: The Papacy, who had sometimes opposed slavery, did not condemn it explicitly to the end of the 17th century; in fact the Church itself has an interest in the colonial system.
The Company of Senegal was in turn founded by Colbert in 1673.
The Black Code, enacted in 1685, regulated the trafficking of slaves in the American colonies.
On 10 February 1763 the Treaty of Paris ended the Seven Years' War and reconciled, after three years of negotiations, France, Great Britain and Spain.
Slavery was abolished by the National Convention in 1794, then reinstated by Napoleon in 1802.
The British Empire abolished slavery in 1833; in France it was finally abolished in the Second Republic in 1848, under the leadership of Victor Schœlcher.

chapters.title: Modern colonialism
chapters.summary: Various European powers – Portugal, the Netherlands, and England – competed for trade in the area from the 15th century onward, until in 1677, France ended up in possession of what had become a minor slave trade departure point—the infamous island of Gorée next to modern Dakar. In 1758 the French settlement was captured by a British expedition as part of the Seven Years' War, but was later returned to France.

events.label: 15th c.
events.text: Various European powers – Portugal, the Netherlands, and England – competed for trade in the area from the 15th century onward, until in 1677, France ended up in possession of what had become a minor slave trade departure point—the infamous island of Gorée next to modern Dakar.
In 1758 the French settlement was captured by a British expedition as part of the Seven Years' War, but was later returned to France.
In 1848, the French Second Republic extended the rights of full French citizenship to their inhabitants.
It was only in the 1850s that the French, under the governor, Louis Faidherbe, began to expand their foothold onto the Senegalese mainland, at the expense of the native kingdoms.
On 2 April 1852 the parliamentary seat for Senegal was abolished by Napoleon III.
Following the downfall of the French Second Empire, the Four Communes was again allowed a parliamentary seat which was granted by law on 1 February 1871.

On 30 December 1875 this seat was again abolished, but only for a few years as it was reinstated on 8 April 1879, and remained the single parliamentary representation from sub-Saharan Africa anywhere in a European legislature until the fall of the third republic in 1940.
Blaise Diagne, who was the prime advocate behind the change, was in 1914 the first African deputy elected to the French National Assembly.
It was only in 1916 that originaires were granted full voting rights while maintaining legal protections.
From that time until independence in 1960, the deputies of the Four Communes were always African, and were at the forefront of the decolonisation struggle.

chapters.title: Independence
chapters.summary: In 1959, Senegal and the French Sudan merged to form the Mali Federation, which became fully independent in 1960. The transfer of power agreement with France was signed on 4 April 1960, commemorated as the Senegalese Independence Day.

events.text: In 1959, Senegal and the French Sudan merged to form the Mali Federation, which became fully independent in 1960.

The Republic of Senegal was formally proclaimed on 5 September 1960, with Léopold Sédar Senghor as President (head of state)—internationally known poet, politician, and statesman—and Mamadou Dia as Prime Minister (president of the 15-member Council of Ministers).
In December 1962, their political rivalry led to an attempted coup by Prime Minister Dia.
Senghor's party, the Senegalese Progressive Union (now the Socialist Party of Senegal), was the only legally permitted party from 1965 until 1975.

In the latter year, Senghor allowed the formation of two opposition parties that began operation in 1976—a Marxist party (the African Independence Party) and a liberal party (the Senegalese Democratic Party).
On 31 December 1980, President Senghor retired from politics, and handed power over to his handpicked successor, Prime Minister Abdou Diouf, 1 January 1981.

chapters.narrative: In 1959, Senegal and the French Sudan merged to form the Mali Federation, which became fully independent in 1960 [S7]. The transfer of power agreement with France was signed on 4 April 1960, commemorated as the Senegalese Independence Day [S7]. The Republic of Senegal was formally proclaimed on 5 September 1960, with Léopold Sédar Senghor as President and Mamadou Dia as Prime Minister [S7]. In December 1962, their political rivalry led to an attempted coup by Prime Minister Dia [S7]. Senghor's party, the Senegalese Progressive Union, was the only legally permitted party from 1965 until 1975 [S7]. On 31 December 1980, President Senghor retired and handed power to Prime Minister Abdou Diouf on 1 January 1981 [S7].

chapters.title: 1980–present
chapters.summary: Senegal joined with The Gambia to form the nominal confederation of Sénégambia on 1 February 1982. However, the envisaged integration of the two countries was never carried out and the union was dissolved in 1989.

events.text: Abdou Diouf was president between 1981 and 2000.
Senegal joined with The Gambia to form the nominal confederation of Sénégambia on 1 February 1982.
However, the envisaged integration of the two countries was never carried out and the union was dissolved in 1989.
In the presidential election of 2000, he was defeated in a free and fair election by opposition leader Abdoulaye Wade.

On 30 December 2004, President Abdoulaye Wade announced that he would sign a peace treaty with two separatist factions of the Movement of Democratic Forces of Casamance (MFDC) in the Casamance region.
As of late 2006, it seemed the peace treaty was holding, as both factions and the Senegalese military appeared to honor the treaty.
"Landscapes of the Slave Trade in Senegal and The Gambia", Focus on Geography (2014) 57#1 pp. 14–24.
In February 2019, president Macky Sall was re-elected and he won a second term.
In March 2024, Opposition candidate Bassirou Diomaye Faye won the Senegal’s presidential election over the candidate of the ruling coalition, becoming the youngest president in Senegal’s history.

chapters.narrative: Abdou Diouf was president between 1981 and 2000 [S8]. Senegal joined with The Gambia to form the nominal confederation of Sénégambia on 1 February 1982, however the envisaged integration of the two countries was never carried out and the union was dissolved in 1989 [S8]. In the presidential election of 2000, he was defeated in a free and fair election by opposition leader Abdoulaye Wade [S8]. On 30 December 2004, President Abdoulaye Wade announced that he would sign a peace treaty with two separatist factions of the Movement of Democratic Forces of Casamance (MFDC) in the Casamance region, and as of late 2006 the treaty seemed to be holding [S8]. In February 2019 president Macky Sall was re-elected to a second term, and in March 2024 opposition candidate Bassirou Diomaye Faye won the presidential election, becoming the youngest president in Senegal's history [S8].
